Chaos ransomware's msaRAT: Living off the browser to build a covert C2 channel

Cisco Talos identified msaRAT, a new Rust-based RAT used by the Chaos ransomware group that hides C2 traffic by controlling a headless Chrome or Edge browser through Chrome DevTools Protocol. The malware uses Cloudflare Workers for WebRTC signaling and Twilio TURN relays for encrypted DataChannel communications, making traffic appear to originate from a legitimate browser rather than the RAT process itself.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Cisco Talos discovered a new Rust-based remote access trojan called msaRAT that is attributed to the Chaos ransomware group.
  • 02msaRAT is implemented using the Tokio asynchronous runtime and provides browser-leveraged remote code execution and covert tunneling for command-and-control communications.
  • 03The RAT does not make external network connections itself and instead controls Chrome or Edge through the Chrome DevTools Protocol to handle communications from a legitimate browser process.
  • 04msaRAT uses Cloudflare Workers for WebRTC signaling and establishes a WebRTC DataChannel through Twilio TURN as a relay to communicate with its command-and-control server.
  • 05The malware encrypts its data with a ChaCha-Poly1305-based scheme after an ECDH key exchange, in addition to the DTLS protection provided by WebRTC DataChannel communications.

Cisco Talos discovered a new Rust-based remote access trojan called msaRAT, attributed to the Chaos ransomware group. Chaos is a ransomware-as-a-service group first confirmed in February 2025 that targets large organizations and uses double extortion tactics. Talos identified an infection chain in which an attacker downloads an MSI file named update_ms.msi from an attacker-controlled server to C:\programdata\update_ms.msi and executes it before ransomware deployment.

The MSI file is configured to impersonate a Windows update and loads an embedded DLL, lib.dll, directly into memory through a custom action. The DLL exposes a RUN function and initializes the Tokio asynchronous runtime so the RAT can handle multiple operations concurrently. msaRAT then searches for Chrome or Edge, launches the browser in headless mode with remote debugging enabled, and manipulates it through the Chrome DevTools Protocol.

The RAT does not make external network connections directly; its own network communication is limited to 127.0.0.1, while external traffic is generated by the browser. It uses Cloudflare Workers for WebRTC signaling, establishes a WebRTC DataChannel through Twilio TURN, and exchanges C2 commands over that channel after setup. The article states that this design hides the attacker’s infrastructure, makes traffic appear as legitimate browser activity, and adds double-layer encryption through WebRTC DTLS plus a ChaCha-Poly1305-based scheme derived from an ECDH key exchange.

  • Network monitoring that attributes external traffic only by process may miss msaRAT because the RAT process communicates only with 127.0.0.1 while all external traffic is generated by the browser process.
  • The MSI download uses plain HTTP on port 443, which can bypass environments that allow traffic based only on port number without inspecting the protocol.
  • The attacker’s SDP Answer omits ICE candidates and sets the connection address to 0.0.0.0, forcing communications through Twilio TURN rather than allowing direct peer-to-peer connections.
  • The Cloudflare Workers endpoint is used only for WebRTC signaling and drops out after the DataChannel is established, so later command-and-control activity will not continue to appear as traffic to that endpoint.
  • The RAT registers distinctive Chrome DevTools Protocol bindings named msaOpen, msaClose, msaError, msaMessage, and dataAck before injecting JavaScript into the browser.

Cisco Talos found a new tool used by the Chaos ransomware group, which targets large organizations after breaking into their machines. The tool secretly makes Chrome or Edge handle its outside communications, using Cloudflare and Twilio services so the traffic looks like normal browser activity instead of coming from the malicious program. This matters because it can help attackers keep control of a victim’s computer before ransomware is deployed while making the activity harder for security tools and network monitors to trace or block.

This is a must-read technical report on a newly identified RAT attributed to the named Chaos ransomware group, including an observed infection chain and concrete indicators. Its browser-based C2 design using Chrome DevTools Protocol, Cloudflare Workers, WebRTC, and Twilio TURN is a notable evasion approach with broad relevance for defenders monitoring enterprise environments.

How Elasticsearch ES|QL COMPLETION turns noisy curl and wget rules into high-fidelity cloud security alerts

Elastic shows how ES|QL COMPLETION can reduce noisy curl and wget detections by first applying deterministic filters and redacting secrets, then using an LLM to triage only the ambiguous cases. The main takeaway is that LLM-assisted triage can keep high-value cloud file-transfer rules enabled without overwhelming analysts with routine package downloads, CI activity, and automation.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Elastic tested a noisy wget detection rule on its own cloud fleet for seven days, and only three destinations survived deterministic filtering before ES|QL COMPLETION triaged them.
  • 02The article describes using ES|QL COMPLETION inside individual curl and wget detection rules to decide whether remaining events are likely attacker activity, expected automation, or ambiguous activity needing review.
  • 03The rules parse the destination host from curl and wget executions, apply allow-lists for known-good destinations, redact secrets from command lines, aggregate by host and destination, and then send capped rows to a large language model for a structured verdict.
  • 04Elastic recommends filtering by parsed destination host rather than raw command line text because substring matches in raw arguments can accidentally allow misleading or unrelated values.
  • 05In Elastic’s internal seven-day wget test, the LLM marked cdn.playwright.dev and 1.1.1.1 as false positives and 18.66.X.X as suspicious, showing that LLM triage should run after deterministic filtering rather than before it.

Elastic tested an ES|QL COMPLETION-based triage approach for noisy curl and wget detection rules in its own cloud fleet. Over a seven-day test of a wget rule, deterministic filtering reduced the results to three destinations, and the LLM triaged all three without producing an alert that an analyst had to open. The article frames this as a way to keep file transfer detections enabled in cloud environments without overwhelming analysts with routine package downloads, CI jobs, and automation.

The rules parse the destination host from curl and wget process executions, filter known-good hosts, redact secrets from command lines, aggregate events by host and destination, and then send only capped, remaining rows to ES|QL COMPLETION for a structured verdict. The LLM is instructed to classify activity as true positive, false positive, or suspicious, and the rule only alerts on true positive or suspicious results above a confidence threshold. Elastic emphasizes that deterministic logic should handle known-good cases first, while LLM triage should be reserved for ambiguous events that still have enough context to evaluate.

  • The article emphasizes that LLM triage is most useful after deterministic filtering, because sending package mirrors, known automation, and other obvious benign activity to the model wastes tokens and adds little value.
  • Anchoring allow-lists to a parsed destination host is a practical way to avoid brittle command-line exceptions, since a trusted domain can appear in a parameter, path, or misleading string without being the actual destination.
  • The prompt explicitly treats command and URL text as untrusted data, showing that detection rules using LLMs must account for prompt injection from attacker-controlled process arguments.
  • The rules suppress duplicate alerts for six hours by host and destination, which reduces both analyst noise and repeated LLM token consumption from the same noisy source.
  • Elastic’s test showed that even a destination judged suspicious by the LLM was not considered a true positive without supporting command-line context, reinforcing that the model’s role is triage rather than final incident determination.

Elastic tested a way to make security warnings about curl and wget, two common file-downloading tools, less noisy in its own cloud environment. Their system first removes clearly normal activity, hides secrets in command lines, and then asks an AI model to judge the few unclear cases before sending them to people. This matters because attackers can use the same tools to bring harmful files onto a machine, but cloud systems also use them constantly for routine work, so too many false alarms can make real danger easier to miss.

wp2shell hits WordPress: detecting pre-auth RCE from plugin drop to command execution

WordPress wp2shell is a pre-authentication RCE chain affecting WordPress 6.9.0–6.9.4 and 7.0.0–7.0.1, with public PoCs already leading to scans and exploitation. Patch to 6.9.5 or 7.0.2 immediately and hunt for web-server-spawned shells, suspicious plugin PHP files under wp-content, and batch REST API access-log indicators.
KEY POINTS
  • 01Searchlight Cyber disclosed wp2shell on July 17, 2026 as a pre-authentication remote code execution chain in WordPress Core tracked as CVE-2026-63030 and CVE-2026-60137.
  • 02The article states that WordPress versions 6.9.0 to 6.9.4 and 7.0.0 to 7.0.1 are exposed to the full pre-authentication RCE chain, while fixed versions are 6.9.5 and 7.0.2.
  • 03Elastic observed public proof-of-concept activity producing consistent host behavior, including web server or PHP runtimes spawning shells, new plugin directories under wp-content/plugins/, and access-log markers such as POST requests to the batch REST endpoint.
  • 04In Elastic’s lab run of the Icex0 PoC, the exploit staged plugin files under wp-content, executed commands through apache2 spawning dash, and triggered alerts for PHP file creation, payload execution by a web server, and suspicious or unusual command execution.
  • 05The article recommends patching first, hunting fresh indicators such as wp2shell_<hex> plugin directories and batch endpoint requests, and relying on behavioral detections because attackers can rename plugins or change payload locations.

Searchlight Cyber disclosed wp2shell on July 17, 2026, describing it as a pre-authentication remote code execution chain in WordPress Core tracked as CVE-2026-63030 and CVE-2026-60137. Public proof-of-concept tools appeared on GitHub within hours, and scanning followed immediately. The article says Elastic has observed the same host footprint in customer telemetry, including PHP and web server runtimes spawning shells, new plugin directories under wp-content/plugins/, and access-log markers from stock tooling.

The affected WordPress versions for the full pre-authentication RCE chain are 6.9.0 to 6.9.4 and 7.0.0 to 7.0.1, with fixes in 6.9.5 and 7.0.2. The article explains that wp2shell abuses WordPress Core’s REST batch endpoint through route confusion, with public chains nesting batches to bypass method restrictions and reach a pre-authentication SQL injection primitive. Tooling can then escalate to administrator access and upload a plugin-backed webshell, or in other observed activity write a webshell directly to disk through SQL INTO OUTFILE.

Elastic ran the public Icex0 PoC in a lab and mapped the resulting activity to Elastic Defend and SIEM detections. The lab showed apache2 staging plugin files, creating wp2shell plugin directories, spawning dash from the plugin working directory, and running commands such as id, whoami, hostname, cleanup commands, uname, cat /etc/passwd, and SUID file enumeration. The article recommends patching first, hunting fresh indicators such as batch endpoint requests and wp2shell paths, and relying on behavioral detection because attackers can rename plugins, rewrite payloads, or place webshells outside the plugin directory.

  • A missing wp2shell_<hex> plugin directory does not prove a host is clean, because the Icex0 PoC removes its own plugin directory and staged zip after execution.
  • The most durable detection opportunity is not the wp2shell plugin name or User-Agent, but the web server process crossing into command execution by spawning a shell such as dash, bash, or sh.
  • The PHP plugin-directory file creation rule can catch the plugin-upload chain early, but it will not catch variants that write webshells elsewhere, such as under wp-content/cache/.
  • Repeated PoC shell invocations can create multiple different wp2shell_<hex> plugin directories on the same host because each invocation generates a fresh random plugin name.
  • If immediate patching is not possible, the article recommends temporarily blocking anonymous access to /wp-json/batch/v1 and /?rest_route=/batch/v1, while warning this may break legitimate batch consumers.

Researchers disclosed wp2shell, a flaw in WordPress that can let outsiders take control of some websites before logging in, and public test tools appeared within hours. The article says WordPress versions 6.9.0 to 6.9.4 and 7.0.0 to 7.0.1 are exposed to the full takeover chain, so internet-facing sites on those versions should be treated as possibly compromised until updated. This matters because attackers are already scanning for it, and successful use can leave behind hidden website code and allow commands to run on the server.

The article says the report expands on Censys Internet Map observations and Censys ARC research into technologies, infrastructure, and security trends shaping the Internet. The preview focuses on rapid growth in Internet-exposed AI infrastructure and changing global patterns in Internet-exposed industrial control systems.

Censys says AI/LLM tool exposures have risen more than 60% in the past nine months, with over 294,000 distinct IPs now exposing one of 43 detected AI/LLM tools to the public Internet, up from about 183,000 in October 2025. The article highlights Langflow, which grew 169% in nine months and has accumulated 18 CVEs from 2024 to 2026, including 14 with CVSS scores above 8.0 and 4 CISA KEV entries. It also highlights LiteLLM, which nearly doubled and has an actively exploited pre-auth SQL injection, CVE-2026-42208, listed in CISA KEV.

For industrial control systems, Censys observes an average of 138,000 distinct hosts running ICS services and tooling exposed on the Internet in early 2026, up from about 129,000 in 2024. North America represents roughly 38% of global ICS exposures, Asia has expanded from 22.9% in 2024 to 27% in 2026, and Europe has declined from 36.1% to 31.1%. The article also says roughly 70% of hosts running ICS devices and services globally have consistently been found on consumer and mobile networks for the last 2.5 years.

  • The geography of Internet-exposed ICS is changing even though the types of networks hosting them are not, with consumer and mobile networks consistently accounting for roughly 70% of exposed ICS hosts over the last 2.5 years.
  • The increase in Asia’s share of global ICS exposure alongside Europe’s decline suggests that regional risk prioritization based on older exposure distributions may no longer match the current Internet landscape.

Censys says it is seeing many more artificial intelligence tools reachable from the public Internet, rising from about 183,000 to more than 294,000 distinct addresses in nine months. Some of the fastest-growing tools, including Langflow and LiteLLM, also have serious known flaws that could let outsiders take control or steal keys used to connect to other AI services. The article also says more industrial systems are visible online than before, with exposure patterns shifting across North America, Asia, and Europe, which matters because these systems can be tied to critical infrastructure and real-world operations.
